messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I am not accustomed to having to worry about numerical accuracy in my coding. However, I'm quickly realizing that I really should be.

I've learned about log_sum_exp trick, and I've been trying to compute things in log-space to avoid numerical underflow. (Any other general tips would be appreciated!)

My main question is: what do I need to know about high-dimensional symmetric matrices? I'd like to compute log determinants and the such. I'd also like to compute quadratic forms. (Presumably, there's a smart way to compute these without inverting the matrix?)

I'm seeing that Stan seems so use the LDLT Factor. Is this what I should read up on?

Thanks very much in advance,
Alp

P.S. This whole discussion began as I realized my algorithms were only stable until dimension = 5. I think this is because Eigen has closed-form implementations of things like determinants up to that dimension. (I may be wrong.) Because when I go to dimension = 6, I seem to lose a lot of numerical stability.

Hi Alp,

Yes, read up on Cholesky factorizations in particular, LDLT is mild generalization of Cholesky which sometimes has better stability.  Internally for things like multi_normal and multi_gp Stan is generally doing what is numerical best practice for log determinants, quadratic forms, etc so they're a good place to look for how to deal with things if you're writing C++ code.  If you have more specific questions definitely ask as, much like the log_sum_exp trick, some of these issues are not well explained or documented anywhere.

The Stan model API that is exposed to users for implementing these things themselves is somewhat limited and may be a bit less optimal both numerically and in terms of efficiency.  Part of that is simply due to a lack of time, although in most cases it's simply not trivial to expose certain types of functionality.  E.G., the LDLT factorization would be very hard to expose to users in an (autodiff) efficient way.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
If you are using a covariance matrix (or precision matrix) as a parameter in a model, then it is much better to reparameterize the model in terms of a Cholesky factor of a covariance matrix (or precision matrix). There are several Cholesky factorizations. The one I am referring to here is the lower-triangular matrix with strictly positive diagonal entries, denoted L, such that L * transpose(L) is equal to the covariance matrix (or precision matrix) of interest. This has as much numerical stability as anything in Stan. However, in most cases, substantive discussion of the model will involve the covariance matrix (or precision matrix) and thus in order to figure out your prior for L, you have to take your prior for the covariance matrix (or precision matrix) and multiply by a fairly simple Jacobian determinant.

If you are talking about a known covariance matrix or something internal that you tune in your algorithm, then it is slightly better to use the LDL' form of the Cholesky factorization, which expresses a covariance matrix in terms of L --- which is lower-triangular and has ones on its diagonal --- and D which is a diagonal matrix with strictly diagonal entries. This form is better for matrices that are singular or nearly singular because Eigen does pivoting to avoid dividing by (nearly) zero. So, really it is PLDL'P' where P is a permutation matrix and you may have to keep track of the P matrix. It isn't necessary to worry about the P matrix in some cases, like solving least squares problems.

The other matrix decompositions, such as QR, eigenvalues / vectors, etc. are either not as fast or not as stable as the Cholesky factorizations, so you wouldn't ordinarily need to use them.

Ben

The quadratic form can be cleaned up a bit,

LLT<MatrixXd> L = H.selfadjointView<Eigen::Lower>().ldlt();

Eigen::VectorXd y = L.solve(x);

The trace is a tricker one and I’m surprised more people don’t write it out more efficiently.  Calling trace will be O(N^{3}) because of the intermediate matrix multiplication, but you can actually do it in O(N^{2}).  In components,

Tr[A . B] = \sum_{ij} A_{ij} B_{ji} = A_{i-} B_{-i}

In other words, the trace is the inner product of the ith row of A with the ith column of B (or the other way around, it doesn’t matter) summed over i.

On Wed, Sep 3, 2014 at 1:58 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> The quadratic form can be cleaned up a bit,

> LLT<MatrixXd> L = H.selfadjointView<Eigen::Lower>().ldlt();

> Eigen::VectorXd y = L.solve(x);
> quad = x.squaredNorm();

This won't work if you're using ldlt(), as you need to divide by the square root of the diagonals of D. I'm guessing you meant to call llt() given the type of L but in that case L.solve() isn't computing what you mean to compute.  You want L.matrixL().solve().  We don't have LLT implemented for autodiff right now, so that's not really an option if autodiff is needed.

If using LDLT and dividing by the square root of the diagonals, it will be faster for simple double/float based arithmetic, but will be slower for autodiff because the square roots and divisions will add extra variables to the autodiff stack.  For autodiff with LDLT the quadratic form as it's in Alps notes is about as good as it gets with our code right now.

>
> The trace is a tricker one and I'm surprised more people don't write it out more efficiently.  Calling trace will be O(N^{3}) because of the intermediate matrix multiplication, but you can actually do it in O(N^{2}).  In components,
>
> Tr[A . B] = \sum_{ij} A_{ij} B_{ji} = A_{i-} B_{-i}
>
> In other words, the trace is the inner product of the ith row of A with the ith column of B (or the other way around, it doesn't matter) summed over i.

It is written explicitly in the case of the inverse wishart because A is the inverse of Sigma so the trace can't easily be computed as a dot product without computing A explicitly.  Numerically it's more stable to compute A . B and then take its trace and it's basically as efficient.

Cheers,
Marcus

The best solution there is probably to recognize that basically everything you want to compute using scalar * A can be computed using A and then rescaling it appropriately.  E.G., (scalar * A) \ b = (1.0/scalar) * (A \ b) or det(scalar * A) = scalar^N * det(A) where N is the size of A.

Alternatively, if you *really* need to update the LDLT, you simply need to rescale the entries of D but I don't know if Eigen's API allows this (matrixD() may be const) and I know for sure that the Stan wrapping of LDLT doesn't.

Cheers,
Marcus

> > Sorry. I should be clearer. (BTW: I appreciate all the help guys -- this is immensely useful.)
> >
> > I have A_old at iteration t-1. It is in LDLT form.
> >
> > I have computed it's gradient. Call it G. I have a closed-form expression for it.
> >
> > I want to compute A_new at iteration t in LDLT form.
> >
> > Currently, it seems like I need to do something like
> >
> > A_new = LDLT<MatrixXd>(A_old.reconstructedMatrix() + G);
> >
> > I guess what I'm asking is: there's no "trick" to avoid that LDLT, right?
>
>
> That's right.  The only possible trick is if you somehow know that G is a rank one update, e.g., G = u u^T for some vector u.  In which case the LDLT factorization can be (relatively) cheaply updated.  However, for a general gradient this is unlikely to be the case.

Or a sequence of rank-one updates, which is still unlikely to be applicable. You don't want to call the reconstructedMatrix() method because that will literally do the multiplication. It is presumably worth the trouble to retain the matrix whose factorization is A_old and add G to that before factoring again.

Also, remember to keep track of the pivoting.

Ben

As we continue refactoring we have come to the point where we want to formalize the interaction with the internal Stan code and the code implemented by the interfaces.

>From a client/service perspective we have two sets of relationships: Stan provides services for the client interfaces, and the interfaces provide implementations of classes (mostly I/O) that can be thought of as services with Stan the client. An immediate answer is to template everything with a Recorder class which gets implemented by the interfaces.  But do we want code outside of services to use such classes (even if they’re templated)?  Or do we want some intermediary structure that keeps the use of such classes in, say, src/services?

We also want to look at reducing model compile time.
libstan.a isn't doing that.

The only reason we build the parsers out
as separate translation units is that Windows chokes on
compiling it header only.  They're usable header only
as well if the compilers get better.  I followed
the pattern outlined in Vandevoorde and Josuttis's book:

  1.  header-only file    .hpp
  2.  definitions file    .def.hpp   (includes 1)
  3.  instantiation file  .cpp       (includes 2)

To use header only, you include (2).

To use standalone, you include (1), but also
compile (3) in its own translation unit and then link it.

I like the basic BUGS organization and would like to see for
each example,

1.  Stan program(s) implementing the model (and variants),

2.  program to simulate data (in R or Python),

    in JSON),

    format, with munging program from original to Stan-readable),

7.  documentation needed to understand the model (LaTeX, text, or HTML),

    manual, from BUGS volume, from book, involving logistic
    regression, application area such as population model, model
    type such as IRT or mark-recapture, etc.)

data output, real data output, doc, and author/copyright holder info
together into some kind of collected "book"-like object or set of
web pages that were easy to browse.

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

As I've been trying to figure out how PyStan can use, for example, the split
rhat and ess facilities from Stan, this caught my attention, it's a recent talk
from cppcon 2014 about the "Hourglass" pattern for interfacing between a C++
library and C/C++ "client" software. It does advocate header-only design but
there are some additional details that look interesting, including the
recommendation that points of contact be limited to C89 + const.

http://www.slideshare.net/StefanusDuToit/cpp-con-2014-hourglass-interfaces-for-c-apis

This seems like a good idea from my perspective!

Best,

-a

lots of issues with vector<vector<double>> for locality.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Preliminary IO Validation in Nomad
messages.body_plain:
Not so much vertical space? :-)

What does validate_input do?

So the idea is that people write code that's templated on
the outside with order, smoothness and validation, then you
invoke it however you want?

Does the explicit instantiation for partials and n_inputs
slow anything down?  I don't know how well the compiler can
inline non-static const values.

Do you really need to do the try/catch in the evaluation of
sqrt?  I'd think that'd really slow things down.  Why doesn't
the function itself just throw?  What can sqrt() do to recover
from its own errors?  Asked another way around, when do the
functions called inside the try ever throw?  I'd think it'd
only be internal memory issues.  You don't want to try to
catch coding errors this way.  Maybe the try/catch can be
part of ValidateIO?  But that'd really clutter up the interface.

- Bob

On Sep 16, 2014, at 6:57 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Here's an example of what a function implementation looks like,
>
>   template <short AutodiffOrder, bool StrictSmoothness, bool ValidateIO>
>
>   inline var<AutodiffOrder, StrictSmoothness, ValidateIO>
>
>     sqrt(const var<AutodiffOrder, StrictSmoothness, ValidateIO>& input) {
>
>
>     // Validate inputs
>
>     if (ValidateIO) {
>
>       double val = input.first_val();
>
>       validate_input(val, "sqrt");
>
>       validate_lower_bound(val, 0, "sqrt");
>
>     }
>
>
>     // Expand expression graph
>
>     const short partials_order = 3;  // Explicit instantiation for readability only
>
>     const unsigned int n_inputs = 1; // Ditto
>
>
>     create_node<unary_var_node<AutodiffOrder, partials_order>>(n_inputs);
>
>
>
>     // Push value
>
>     double val = std::sqrt(input.first_val());
>
>
>     try {
>
>       push_dual_numbers<AutodiffOrder, ValidateIO>(val);
>
>     } catch(nomad_error& e) {
>
>       throw nomad_output_value_error("sqrt");
>
>     }
>
>
>     // Push input edges
>
>     push_inputs(input.dual_numbers());
>
>
>     // Push partials
>
>     double d2 = 1.0 / input.first_val();
>
>
>     try {
>
>       if (AutodiffOrder >= 1) push_partials<ValidateIO>(val *= 0.5 * d2);
>
>       if (AutodiffOrder >= 2) push_partials<ValidateIO>(val *= - 0.5 * d2);
>
>       if (AutodiffOrder >= 3) push_partials<ValidateIO>(val *= - 1.5 * d2);
>
>     } catch(nomad_error& e) {
>
>       throw nomad_output_partial_error("sqrt");
>
>     }
>
>
>
>     return var<AutodiffOrder, StrictSmoothness, ValidateIO>(next_node_idx_ - 1);
>
>
>   }
>
>
>

>
>
>
> Anyone have any thoughts or alternative suggestions?

messages.body_plain:
> Not so much vertical space? :-)

-________________________________-

> What does validate_input do?

Checks for nan, throws if necessary,

  inline void validate_input(double val, std::string f_name) {

    std::cout << "Trying to validate input value " << val << std::endl;

    if (unlikely(std::isnan(val))) throw nomad_input_error(f_name);

    else return;

  }

> So the idea is that people write code that's templated on
> the outside with order, smoothness and validation, then you
> invoke it however you want?

People write functors templated against a var type; when you want to instantiate
a  functor you can set order, smoothness, and validation yourself or use one of
the fine typedefs that keep everything hidden away.

> Does the explicit instantiation for partials and n_inputs
> slow anything down?  I don't know how well the compiler can
> inline non-static const values.

Not that I can tell but we can always go through and remove them if someone
can detect a nontrivial difference.

> Do you really need to do the try/catch in the evaluation of
> sqrt?  I'd think that'd really slow things down.  Why doesn't
> the function itself just throw?  What can sqrt() do to recover
> from its own errors?  Asked another way around, when do the
> functions called inside the try ever throw?  I'd think it'd
> only be internal memory issues.  You don't want to try to
> catch coding errors this way.  Maybe the try/catch can be
> part of ValidateIO?  But that'd really clutter up the interface.

Ah, sorry, I didn't describe this thoroughly.  The try block is to catch exceptions
thrown from push_dual_numbers and push_partials which will check for NaNs
upon request (via the ValidateIO template parameter).  This allows us to immediately
identify where the NaN first arises (push_dual_numbers and push_partials wrapped
separately to be able to distinguish the two).

Everything WAS header only in the first place.  Then we ran into slow compilation
times and troubles with Windows toolchains crashing (and maybe other issues?).

You'll have to get more help from Daniel and/or Marcus on the justification
for what's there now --- they both understand the build process much better than
I do.

If var_stack is the only thing left, you should just be able to include the .cpp
like it was a .hpp file.  If it has a header guard, that is.  Adding a header
guard won't hurt it if it doesn't.

The most general way to lay things out is to create three parallel files:

   .hpp       header
   .def.hpp   header-only definitions
   .cpp       instantiations

Then we can have our cake and eat it, too.  To use the lib header only, you
include def.hpp.  To build it, you use .cpp and then for code that links to it,
include .hpp.  It's the code pattern you see in the parser.  It's discussed
in Vandevoorde and Josuttis's most excellent C++ templates book.

- Bob

Brilliant!  Works like a charm.  This is much better
converging and much better mixing once converged.  Roughly
1 effective sample every 1--3 draws across all parameters.

I'll try to make this standard operating procedure.

It's a little less intensive on the multiplies with

  diag_pre_multiply(sigma_Sigma, L_Sigma) * z

instead of

  diag_pre_multiply(sigma_Sigma, L_Sigma * z)

because they are (3 x 1), (3 x 3) and (3 x M) respectively.
Eigen's clever enough to figure this all out on its own
using expression templates, but Stan's not that clever.

It would be more efficient with a diag_pre_multiply_lower_tri()
function.  In fact, we pretty much need a whole bunch of
specializations of matrix ops for:

    diagonal matrices (as vectors)
    symmetric matrices
    lower-triangular (upper-triangular) matrices
    symmetric, positive definite matrices
    correlation matrices ?

This is a nice modular project someone could take on a little
bit at a time that'd make a big difference in multivariate modeling
speed.

Here's the full Ben trick, isolated for inspection:

  parameters {
    matrix[3,M] z;
    vector[3] gamma;
    cholesky_factor_corr[3] L_Sigma;
    vector<lower=0>[3] sigma_Sigma;
    ...
  transformed parameters {
     matrix[M,3] alpha;
     alpha <- transpose(rep_matrix(gamma,M)
                        + diag_pre_multiply(sigma_Sigma, L_Sigma) * z);
  }
  model {
    to_vector(z) ~ normal(0,1);

which produces the equivalent of

  parameters {
    vector[3] gamma;
    cholesky_factor_corr[3] L_Sigma;
    vector<lower=0>[3] sigma_Sigma;
    matrix[M,3] alpha;
    ...
  model {
    alpha ~ multi_normal(gamma,
                         diag_matrix(sigma_Sigma)
                         * L_sigma
                         * L_sigma'
                         * diag_matrix(sigma_Sigma));

(I just wrote the latter version this way for clarity --- quad_form_diag
and multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose would be more efficient.)

Ideally, to make this standard practice, we'd want a function
with behavior defined by

  vector ben_transform(vector mu,
                       vector sigma,
                       matrix L,
                       matrix z) {
    // validate sizes
    return transpose(rep_matrix(mu,cols(z))
                     + diag_pre_multiply(sigma, L) * z);

  }

But we could write it in C++ with the derivatives all done
analytically.

It's tempting, but I think not worthwhile to wrap the whole
thing up with the priors on L and sigma.  For example, we've been
working with models that place distinct informative priors on elements
of sigma.

- Bob

messages.subject: error tolerance for integrate_ode?
messages.body_plain:
Right now, the error tolerance in the ODE solvers are set to
1e-6 absolute and 1e-6 relative.

Question 1:  Why would we ever want an absolute tolerance?
  Can I just make it the max double value?

Question 2:  Can we just stick with 1e-6 relative tolerance, which is
   what all the Boost examples use and pretty close to what everyone
   seems to use for all these integrators across packages.  It seems
   like 1e-6 is plenty of tolerance for stats, but I'm not an ODE
   solving expert.

The error control is now for both the system itself and the
sensitivities (derivatives of solutions w.r.t. parameters).

Currently we have a single function w/o any user-specified tolerances:

   integrate_ode(...);

To allow control of both tolerances we'ed need three
more functions since there's ambiguity in dropping
arguments.  For example,

   integrate_ode_tol(..., abs_tol, rel_tol)

   integrate_ode_abstol(..., abs_tol)

   integrate_ode_reltol(..., rel_tol)

Question 3:  Do we need these?

Question 4:  If so, can we put off adding the tolerances until later
   or are these dealbreakers?

If the answer to (3) is yes, we could use suggestions on how to test.
Do we just set up some equations, set different tolerances, and check the
ODEs determinstically?

- Bob

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/tree/feature/very-experimental-makefix
